title: Glivenko’s theorem and stable propositions

based_on.title: Intuitionistic Logic (ILLC report PP-2006-25; ESSLLI 2005 lectures)
based_on.pages: Section 3.3 printed p. 16, maximal-world double negation; section 3.5 Exercise 32.

summary: Classical propositional consequences become intuitionistic after double negation, and stable conclusions need no translation.
abstract: Classical logic proves excluded middle, while intuitionistic logic proves its double negation. Glivenko’s theorem says this happens for every classical propositional theorem. We explain why a finite ordered countermodel would have a maximal world behaving like an ordinary Boolean assignment, then use this fact to obtain the intuitionistic proof. A formula whose double negation can be removed can consequently be deduced intuitionistically whenever it follows classically from the same finite assumptions. This identifies the earlier negative translation with double negation up to intuitionistic equivalence and makes precise a syntactic family on which the translation can be removed. Counterexamples show why disjunctions and lost premises need separate care.
